lesson_title: Where Did the Log Go? Why Mass Is Never Lost
hook_text: Burn a log and only a little ash is left. Not one atom of it was destroyed.
clip_script: Burn a log and you are left with a handful of ash. Burn magnesium ribbon in a dish and the white powder weighs more than the metal did. So is mass appearing and disappearing? Never. In a chemical reaction atoms only swap partners. Not one is made, not one is destroyed. The log's missing mass floated up the chimney as invisible carbon dioxide and water vapour. The magnesium's extra mass is oxygen from the air that joined on. Close the box, seal the reaction in a container on a scale, and the reading never moves. That is the law of conservation of mass, proved by Lavoisier more than 200 years ago. It is also why chemists count atoms. In an equation, the big number in front says how many molecules; the little number inside says what each molecule is made of. 2H2O: two molecules, two hydrogens each, so four hydrogens. Count every atom on each side. They must match.
visual_style: A log burning down to ash while ghostly CO2 and water molecules drift upward; magnesium powder on a scale ticking up as red oxygen balls join; a sealed jar on a scale holding steady; atoms ticked off on both sides of an equation.
pacing: Two puzzles at speed, a beat of revelation for each, a calm sealed-jar moment, a counting finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and do a full atom stocktake on the gas-stove equation.
